analysis.one_liner: Extends do-not-call protections to every phone, including cell phones, and makes it easier to sue robocallers.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to committee and a subcommittee and never received a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today's federal do-not-call rules officially protect only landline (residential) numbers, and a person can sue an unwanted caller only after receiving multiple calls from the same company within a year. This bill would remove both limits: the do-not-call rules would cover every telephone subscriber, and a single unwanted call from a company would be enough to sue for damages. The FCC would have 270 days to update its regulations to match. The bill was introduced in March 2024 and never moved beyond committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a cell phone, since robocallers and telemarketers could no longer claim cell phones fall outside the do-not-call rules. Consumers who receive scam or spam calls would gain a clearer right to sue after a single call, giving callers a stronger financial reason to stop.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cell phone users and scam-call targets

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the word 'residential' from the do-not-call provisions, extending those protections from landline numbers to all telephone subscribers, including cell phone users [S2].
Changes the private right of action so that one call by or on behalf of an entity, rather than more than one call within a 12-month period, is enough to sue [S2].
Requires the FCC to revise its do-not-call regulations within 270 days of enactment to implement the expanded scope [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketers and companies that make large volumes of sales or solicitation calls would face the full do-not-call regime on cell phones and greater exposure to consumer lawsuits, including from a single unwanted call.

drawbacks.text: Expanding coverage to all subscribers could sweep in calls many people want or need, such as appointment reminders, school notifications, or other informational calls, unless callers take care to stay within exemptions [S2].
Letting a single unwanted call support a lawsuit would increase litigation exposure for businesses that call customers, raising costs that could be passed on to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: robocalls are a persistent consumer nuisance and a vehicle for scams, and closing the cell-phone gap plus the one-call lawsuit threshold gives consumers meaningful leverage. The costs fall on legitimate callers who would need to adjust their practices and on businesses facing more lawsuits, so the bill's design is aggressive but aimed at a genuine problem.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittee without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on March 20, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1, S4].
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where it stayed [S4].
The bill drew only one cosponsor and received no further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S3, S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telemarketers and mass-calling operations, including scammers, are better off because the bill died: the do-not-call regime still formally covers only residential numbers, and consumers still must receive multiple calls within a year before they can sue.

for.name: Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend do-not-call rules to all phone subscribers and expand the private right of action.

for.name: 1 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members joined.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce and took no further action, never scheduling a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: Only the Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor ever signed on, so the record shows no meaningful partisan test of support.

industries.note: These callers profit from reaching consumers by phone and would have faced the do-not-call rules on cell phones for the first time, plus lawsuits after a single unwanted call. Their interest runs against consumers' interest in fewer unwanted calls.

Illegal robocallers currently exploit the fact that cell phones sit outside the formal do-not-call regime and that consumers face a multi-call threshold before suing. The bill would have closed both openings.
